title: Hillsdale Goes To War On Education
author: Peter Greene
summary: Greene reads Hillsdale president Larry Arnn's Imprimis speech, "Education as a Battleground," closely and critically, treating it as a window into the religious right's education manifesto. He follows Arnn's chain of argument from the question of who owns children through the natural family, the administrative state and the claim that schools supplant parents. Along the way he points out contradictions, a dismissal of phonics, and a view of legitimacy as adherence to Truth rather than democratic process. His own position is that parents matter but are not automatically wise, and that choice policies often shift power to private vendors rather than parents. He concludes that Hillsdale's allies want government out of education and are unwilling to negotiate. The piece fits Practice & Culture as Greene's school-policy commentary.
points: Greene argues that Arnn's war language reveals his worldview more than it describes the actual conflict in schools.
He rebuts the premise that anyone who has a child is automatically endowed with sound judgment about that child's schooling.
He catches Arnn endorsing a view of reading that treats learning to read as unassisted and natural, which he says conflates speech with literacy.
The administrative-state critique is partly interesting to him but would apply equally to the choice movement, which moves power to private vendors.
His conclusion is that the Hillsdale camp should be taken at its word: it intends to replace public governance of education and is not seeking compromise.
quotes: I am not a fan of war-and-violence rhetoric. The word "war" has been thrown around a lot as a political tool, and its use in so many causes minimizes actual warfare, in which people try to kill each other and plenty of death and maiming ensues.

Look, I'm a parent four times over, and have been through more than a few experiences in which I have felt the need to make sure my judgment overrules the judgment of the school or the people in it. But the notion that anybody who makes a baby is naturally imbued with common sense and love for that child--well, it is not aligned with reality.

Hey, look! Arnn supports Balanced Literacy and thinks phonics are bunk! Also, Arnn doesn't grasp that learning to speak and learning to read and write are two completely different things, one largely natural and one largely not.

What distinguishes these groups is their remarkably low level of success. And meanwhile, teachers are just trying to "social engineer" students to bring a pencil to class and keep their hands to themselves.

The result has been to move money and authority away from the schools and toward the bureaucracy. It's an interesting observation that puts Arnn directly at odds with the standards movement, and ought to prompt a serious conversation about the choice movement, which pretends to put power in the hands of parents but actually moves it to private vendors and leaves an awful lot of it with the government.
This is one of those times when it's wise not to lump education reformers together. The Hillsdale crowd is really at odds with some reformsters, like every federal approach from NCLB onward.
